reader.title: Killing of T. C. Yates
bases: The wire describes Yates being shot dead when a crowd he had fired into returned fire (A1, A2, A5); only a one-line brief calls the killers a mob (A7).

Yates was killed, but every fuller report says he died when people in a crowd returned the fire he had opened on them, not as punishment under a claim of justice or tradition (A1, A2, A5); the number who fired is not stated, and the single 'killed by a mob' line (A7) reads as a condensation of the same wire and adds no detail.

Two differently worded versions of the Little Rock dispatch agree that Yates was shot in the Chickasaw Nation after firing into a crowd (A1, A2, A5, A11); the Maysville brief's 'mob' (A7) differs on how he was killed but not on the killing itself.

summary.text: The killing of T. C. Yates was the shooting of a man described as "a noted desperado" in the Chickasaw Nation, Indian Territory, on or about September 1, 1888.
According to a wire dispatch from Little Rock, Arkansas, Yates fired into a crowd, people in the crowd fired back, and he fell dead from his horse.
Papers across the country printed the item as a short brief, and one Kentucky paper condensed it to a line saying he had been "killed by a mob."

The dispatch, sent from St. Louis on September 2 as "a special from Little Rock," said Yates had been shot and killed in the Chickasaw Nation "yesterday," and the Rock Island Daily Argus version put the shooting on "Saturday," September 1.
No town, cause of quarrel or name of anyone in the crowd was given.
In the dispatch's words, Yates "wantonly fired into a crowd," the fire was returned, and he "dropped from his horse dead."
A second wording, datelined Little Rock, September 3, said he fell "riddled with bullets."
No report of an inquest, arrests or any later inquiry appears in the coverage, and Yates's race is not stated in any of the reports.
White papers carried the story from September 3 to 7, 1888, nearly always as a single paragraph among telegraphic briefs.

The St. Louis wording ran in the Wheeling Register, the Memphis Appeal, the Indianapolis Journal and the San Antonio Daily Light, while the Little Rock wording appeared in Waterbury, Wilmington, Rock Island and Yankton.
The same item reached weeklies such as the Big Sandy News, the Hickman Courier and the Russellville Democrat later in the week.
Headlines cast the death as the deserved end of an outlaw: "One Desperado Less" in Wheeling, "A Desperado's Last Act" in Waterbury and Wilmington, and "Killed at His Own Game" in Memphis.
The Maysville Evening Bulletin alone changed the substance, reporting in its "Pointed Paragraphs" column that Yates "was killed by a mob in the Chickasaw nation."
The reports differ on how Yates died: most describe return fire from a crowd he had shot into, while the Maysville brief calls the killers "a mob" and gives no other detail.
The Maysville line appeared a day after the fuller dispatch and reads as a condensation of it.
The date also varies, since a weekly news summary printed in the Brookhaven Leader placed the shooting "on the 2d," the date of the original dispatch, rather than on the previous day.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'One Desperado Less' and 'A Desperado's Last Act' presented the shooting as the fitting end of a 'noted desperado' who had fired 'wantonly' into a crowd.
Most papers ran the dispatch as a one-paragraph item in columns of telegraphic briefs, from Memphis and Indianapolis to San Antonio and Yankton.
The Maysville Evening Bulletin compressed the story to one line saying Yates was 'killed by a mob'.

versions.value: Shot when the crowd Yates fired into returned fire

conflicts.note: The return-fire account is the fuller wire text and appeared in many papers a day earlier; the one-line Maysville item adds no detail and looks like a condensation of it.

conflicts.note: The daily dispatches, dated Sept. 2 and printed Sept. 3, are closer to the event than the weekly summary that gives 'the 2d', which probably took the dispatch date for the event date.
